text: Benedek Folhoffer / Age: 24
Rank/Position: Private (enlisted soldier), assistant machine gunner (ammunition bearer)
Civilian Occupation: Carpenter's apprentice
Origin: Near Győr, Transdanubia
If for nothing else, Folhoffer Benedek was grateful for this:
out here, in the middle of this frozen hell,
nobody knew he had killed his mother.
He hadn't meant to, of course.
A breech-born infant doesn't have bloodlust or anything like that.
But whatever happened, happened.
His mother bled out.
And Benedek's father declared him
his sworn enemy
about six and a half minutes after he entered the world.
Benedek grew up hearing it, over and over.
That he was a little murderer. A cursed child.
Not everyone said it to hurt him. Some said it as a fact. Some like a joke.
His paternal grandfather was even proud.
Proud that Benedek had barely drawn his first breath
and already put a Swab in the ground.
But his father never softened. Not for a second.
It was too bitter a pill to swallow
that his son had made him a widower.
Benedek waited until he was fourteen.
Then he left Mezőörs behind.
He took money from weaker kids by force.
He bought a train ticket. He didn't stop until Tata,
where he found work as a carpenter's apprentice.
He had as much natural talent for wood
as a fattened pig has for self-restraint.
But what God had denied him in skill,
he made up for with stubbornness.
His grandfather used to say it all the time.
Not the clever ones get ahead in life,
but the ones who can sit still and learn.
He'd say it under the shade of the cabinet, cherries in their mouths,
counting on an abacus while the sun hammered the yard.
As it turned out, the old man was right.
At first, Master Trokán Pista only respected Benedek's effort.
The fact that he showed up day after day. That he didn't quit.
Then, slowly, he began to respect the work itself.
Once in a while, he'd even say something kind.
“You're not as hopeless as you look,” he'd tell him,
clapping him on the shoulder. And Benedek swelled with pride.
Around that time, he decided to take
his dead mother's surname as well. Folhoffer.
When he walked out of the registrar's office,
for the first time in his life he stopped thinking of himself as a killer.
But now… <i>“Now I've finally become
what my dear father always said I was,”
Benedek mutters as he drops back into the trench for a few seconds to breathe.
The endless white is hurting his sight.
Stars dance in front of his eyes. Snow-blindness makes him doubt everything.
He can't even be sure he hit anyone across the river.
And yet he feels it. He feels that he isn't just shooting into the world at random.
Because lately it has been getting harder to think of himself as a carpenter.
Harder to hold onto that word. As if the soul can sense its own slow destruction even when the senses begin to fail.
To keep from focusing only on the cold besieging his limbs and joints, Benedek tries to distract himself from everything around him
by wondering whether he will ever be able to create
another table or another door, if he ever makes it home.
Can a hand still create, after months of doing nothing but destroy?
